notation.meaning: Vector of weights on the columns
Regressors, coefficients and fitted values in the regression reading
Vectors (e.g. columns of a data matrix)
Projection (hat) matrix: turns $\mathbf{y}$ into fitted values
Non-labor income, labor income and total income ($T = NI + S$) in the example

blocks.md: **Regression is a projection. $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}$ is a point in the column space of $\mathbf{X}$; OLS picks the one closest to $\mathbf{y}$; the residual is what is left, orthogonal to every regressor. Rank decides whether that point corresponds to a unique $\mathbf{b}$.**

sections.heading: 1. A matrix times a vector is a combination of columns

blocks.md: [Column Space](note:column-space): $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b} = b_1\mathbf{x}_1 + \dots + b_K\mathbf{x}_K$. Every possible fitted vector lives in $\mathrm{col}(\mathbf{X})$. With $N > K$, $\mathbf{y}$ is almost never in it, so there is no exact fit — only a closest one.

[Linear Independence and Rank](note:linear-independence-and-rank): if the columns are independent, different $\mathbf{b}$ give different fitted vectors, so the closest point pins down a unique $\mathbf{b}$. If a column is a combination of others (total income = labor + non-labor income; all dummies plus a constant) the rank drops and $\mathbf{b}$ is not identified — the [Full Rank and Identification](note:full-rank-and-identification) condition in [Econ 430 L7 The Classical Linear Regression Model](note:econ-430-l7-the-classical-linear-regression-model).

[Inner Products and Orthogonality](note:inner-products-and-orthogonality): "closest" means the residual is perpendicular to the column space, $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$ — exactly the normal equations. The same geometry says a correlation is the cosine of an angle, and Cauchy–Schwarz is why it lies in $[-1, 1]$.

blocks.prompt: Which condition picks out the closest point $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}$ to $\mathbf{y}$?

options.feedback: With $N > K$, $\mathbf{y}$ is almost never in $\mathrm{col}(\mathbf{X})$, so no $\mathbf{b}$ fits exactly; the closest point still leaves a nonzero residual.

options.md: The residual is orthogonal to every column of $\mathbf{X}$: $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$
The columns of $\mathbf{X}$ are orthogonal to each other
options.feedback: That is a property of the regressors, not of $\mathbf{b}$, so it cannot pick out a point; correlated regressors still have a closest point.

The residual is perpendicular to the column space, where the fitted vector lives, not to $\mathbf{y}$ itself: $\mathbf{y}$ is the fitted vector plus $\mathbf{e}$, so it has a component along $\mathbf{e}$.

blocks.why: "Closest" means the residual $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}$ is perpendicular to the column space, so it is orthogonal to every column $\mathbf{x}_k$: $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$. Those $K$ equations are exactly the normal equations.

blocks.md: [Projection Matrix and Residual Maker](note:projection-matrix-and-residual-maker): $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'$ does the projecting and $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$ produces the residuals. The simplest case — projecting onto a single vector, or onto the constant — shows that demeaning a variable is itself a projection. Partialling out a trend in [Econ 424 L2 Between-Group Inequality](note:econ-424-l2-between-group-inequality) is the same operation with $\mathbf{X}_1 = [\mathbf{1}, t]$.

blocks.prompt: Slide a point along $\mathbf{a}$ until the residual is as short as possible
blocks.purpose: See that the closest point to b on the line through a is where the residual is orthogonal to a, and that it sits at t = (a.b)/(a.a)

blocks.prompt: 1. Is $\mathbf{b} = (1,2,4)'$ in the column space of $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$?

options.feedback: $x = (1, 2)'$ matches the first two entries, but the third entry it gives is $1 + 2 = 3$, not 4. Every entry has to match.

options.md: Yes: two independent columns reach every vector with three entries
options.feedback: Two columns span only a plane inside three-dimensional space, so most vectors with three entries lie off it.

options.md: No: the weights that match the first two entries give the wrong third entry

blocks.why: No. Matching the first two rows needs $x = (1, 2)'$, which gives a third entry of 3, not 4. → [Column Space](note:column-space)

blocks.prompt: 1b. There is no exact fit, so take the closest one: the least-squares fit of $\mathbf{b} = (1,2,4)'$ on the two columns of that matrix. What is its residual sum of squares?

wrong.md: that is the miss from fitting the first two entries exactly with $x = (1, 2)'$; least squares spreads the miss over all three entries
that is the length of the residual, $\sqrt{1/3}$; the sum of squares is its square

blocks.why: The least-squares solution is $(4/3, 7/3)'$, so the fitted vector is $(4/3, 7/3, 11/3)'$ and the residual $(-1/3, -1/3, 1/3)'$, with residual sum of squares $3 \times 1/9 = 1/3$. → [Column Space](note:column-space)

blocks.prompt: 2. What is the rank of $[\mathbf{1},\ NI,\ S,\ NI + S]$?

wrong.md: that counts the columns; the fourth is the sum of the second and third, so it adds no new direction

blocks.why: 3: the fourth column is the sum of the second and third. → [Linear Independence and Rank](note:linear-independence-and-rank)

blocks.prompt: 3. Project $\mathbf{b} = (3, 1)'$ onto $\mathbf{a} = (1, 1)'$. Which vector do you get?

options.feedback: That is $(\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{b})\,\mathbf{a}$ with $\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{b} = 4$: you still need to divide by $\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{a} = 2$.
That divides $\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{b} = 4$ by the length $\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert = \sqrt{2}$; the projection divides by $\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{a} = 2$.
That is the residual, the part of $\mathbf{b}$ orthogonal to $\mathbf{a}$; the projection is the part along $\mathbf{a}$.

blocks.why: $\frac{\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{a} = 2\,(1,1)' = (2,2)'$; residual $(1,-1)'$, orthogonal to $\mathbf{a}$. → [Projection Matrix and Residual Maker](note:projection-matrix-and-residual-maker)

blocks.prompt: 4. For $\mathbf{x} = (1,2,3,4,5)'$ and $\mathbf{y} = (2,1,4,3,6)'$, what is the cosine of the angle between the demeaned vectors?

wrong.md: that uses the raw vectors; demean both first (the means are 3 and 3.2)

that divides $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}'\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = 10$ by $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}'\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = 10$ only; the cosine divides by both lengths, $\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\rVert\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\rVert$
that is $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}'\tilde{\mathbf{y}}/4$, the sample covariance; the cosine divides by the two lengths instead

blocks.why: Demeaned, $\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (-2,-1,0,1,2)'$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = (-1.2,-2.2,0.8,-0.2,2.8)'$, so $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}'\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = 10$, $\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\rVert = \sqrt{10}$ and $\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\rVert = \sqrt{14.8}$. The cosine is $10/\sqrt{148} = 0.822$ — which is the sample correlation. → [Inner Products and Orthogonality](note:inner-products-and-orthogonality)

blocks.prompt: 5. Why can adding a regressor never lower $R^2$?

options.md: It enlarges the column space, so the closest point to $\mathbf{y}$ can only get closer
The new regressor's coefficient is never zero, so it always explains some extra variation
options.feedback: Its coefficient can be exactly zero, and then the fit is unchanged. The argument has to cover that case too.

options.md: The new column already lies in the old column space, so it cannot pull the fit away from $\mathbf{y}$
options.feedback: A column inside the old column space is a combination of the old columns: the rank would not rise and the fit would not change at all. A new regressor usually adds a direction.

blocks.why: It enlarges the column space, so the closest point to $\mathbf{y}$ can only get closer. → [Column Space](note:column-space)

sections.heading: What to be able to do

blocks.md:
1. Read $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}$ as a linear combination of columns.
2. Find the rank of a design matrix and spot exact linear dependence.
3. Explain the normal equations as an orthogonality condition.
4. Compute a projection onto a vector and onto a column space.
